name: Victor Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Victor, 43. I finished secondary school and came into paid music late, so I am still the junior rhythm guitarist at a small events firm. I play simple parts, record rough demos and teach two beginners after school; I like seeing a child land a clean chord, but late notices about cancelled jobs wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who depends on that income, and what happens in a lean week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lina works part-time at a grocery shop, and we have a 12-year-old and an eight-year-old. The mortgage takes the first bite, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. There are few music jobs nearby; the firm pays me less than the lead players because I am still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the other guitarists that the big promises came to little, and we'd better make the next set sound good. A program sorting bookings won't fix a thin fee for a late wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is already close to the edge, even if AI changes almost nothing. Lina's shop hours go up and down, and I cannot cover a month without work from savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the firm's weekend dates and the two beginner lessons. Starting now I'd ask for next month's bookings in writing, and through the first year I'd put any extra lesson fee toward the overdue electricity bill before buying music gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because normal life is enough to make us count coins. I am glad there is no new blow, but a quiet weekend is still a blow to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which payment becomes difficult first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The electricity bill slips first, and then I worry about the mortgage notice. We can miss a takeaway; we cannot miss the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about a cancelled job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children there was no show this weekend and we will go to the free park instead. I would not make them carry the whole worry, but they notice when I say no to a school trip.

say: I would tell the guitarists to focus on the **next set** despite loud AI claims.
I would say booking software cannot fix a **thin fee** for a late wedding.
think: The **mortgage** and Lina’s uneven shop hours already make a quiet weekend risky.
Less than a **month saved** leaves no safe gap between bookings.
do: Keep the firm’s **weekend dates** and two beginner lessons through the first year.
Ask for **next-month bookings** in writing now.
Put extra **lesson fees** toward electricity arrears before buying gear.
feel: I feel **anxious** because ordinary slow weeks already threaten the bills.
S0.quote: We can miss a takeaway; we cannot miss the roof.
fieldNote: His **thin cushion** and variable household wages make the plateau stressful without dramatic AI change.
He is a **junior player** still learning, with few comparable jobs nearby.

steps.text: Keep firm weekend dates and two beginner lessons
Put extra lesson fees toward overdue electricity bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software can help the office, but I want the firm to say plainly if it is buying fewer demos and lessons. I would ask the local musicians' group to demand notice before hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rough demo pays less than a full show, yet losing two a month would take away our grocery money. Beginner pupils might also use an app; I am not a famous teacher they will wait for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask the firm which paid dates are firm and check the two pupils' bookings with their parents. In the first year, if demos drop, I'd stop renting the rehearsal locker, ask the musicians' group about written notice, and take a paid evening shift at the grocer only if there is an opening that fits Lina's childcare hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed. Our bills do not get smaller because someone says workers have time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a lost demo fee do at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two missing demos take about a week's food from our plan. I would ask Lina which shop shifts she could swap, but I would not assume she can pick up more hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new software if the firm offered it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI tools, and I would not start on the firm's promise alone. If the firm paid for training during work hours and showed that the tool kept my paid dates, I would watch a colleague try it first.

I would ask the local **musicians’ group** to speak for casual players.
think: Two missing **demos** could take a week of grocery money.

Cancel the **rehearsal locker** if demos drop in the first year.

feel: I feel **alarmed** because a small fee loss would land on basic bills.

fieldNote: He avoids **AI tools** and would only observe training if paid work time and dates were protected.
The **grocery shift** depends on a real opening and childcare, while demos supply food money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm that thinking AGI by 2028 could do the demo planning and beginner coaching first. Robots able to play guitar follow around 2031. Three extra years before robot guitarists arrive do not pay this mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cheap demo work could go almost at once, and parents might stop the lessons. Lina's part-time shop wage cannot cover the mortgage, food and two children's needs by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I'd get a written list of our monthly bills and ask the musicians' group about notice and support. In the first year after AGI arrives, if the firm cuts my dates, I'd cancel the rehearsal locker, ask the lender for a temporary payment plan before missing a mortgage payment, and apply for the posted school caretaker job if it is still open. I would keep paid lessons until a real job offer comes, and ask the school office about other paid maintenance work if the caretaker post is filled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed and awake at night. I have a list of calls to make, but less than a month's savings leaves no room for a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do the week the firm stopped calling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the firm for a written account of cancelled dates, then call the lender before the due date. If the caretaker post has gone, I would ask the school office what other paid maintenance work exists, not say I have a job lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help before the mortgage payment is late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina could ask her manager about one extra shift, but only if someone can pick up the children. I would ask my sister to help with a school pickup first, not ask her to pay our mortgage.

I would tell the firm that extra years of **hands-on work** do not cover the mortgage.
think: Demo work and beginner lessons could **disappear quickly**.
Lina’s **part-time wage** cannot cover the family mortgage and food alone.
do: List **monthly bills** and ask the musicians’ group about notice before 2028.
Cancel locker if dates fall and ask lender for a plan before missing payment in first year after **2028**.
Apply for **open caretaker work** if dates fall; if filled, ask the school office about other paid work while keeping lessons.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and short of time despite having calls to make.
S2.quote: Three extra years before robot guitarists arrive do not pay this mortgage.
fieldNote: He expects **thinking work** to vanish in 2028, before robot guitarists arrive around 2031.
His **caretaker search** needs a real vacancy; otherwise he asks about paid maintenance work and keeps lessons until offered a job.

Ask lender before missed mortgage payment in first year after 2028 if firm dates fall
Apply for open caretaker post in first year after 2028 if firm dates fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the musicians' group that five years is enough to ask for fair notice and a real path to another paid job. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031, while guitar-playing robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish a basic building-maintenance certificate before the demos are undercut. I cannot pay tuition or miss weekend fees just to hold a certificate that no nearby employer wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the local school whether its caretaker vacancies require a maintenance certificate. If the school confirms it and a training grant covers tuition with classes outside paid gig hours, I'd enrol before 2031; in the first year after AGI arrives, I'd apply for a posted caretaker vacancy if music dates fall, while keeping paid lessons that remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives me a calendar instead of a scramble. The mortgage still runs every month while I study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you learn in five years with your family bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the school office for the actual job requirements and the training centre for the full fee. If the grant fails, I would keep playing paid dates and look for a different local opening rather than borrow for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave music if training led to paid work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I would take a paid caretaker job if it fits the school run and covers our bills. I would still play the weekend dates that pay, because changing work does not mean throwing away every song.

I would distinguish **2031 thinking AGI** from capable robot players around 2034.
think: A **maintenance certificate** might help if a nearby employer requires it.

fieldNote: He ties **retraining** to a real employer requirement, grant money and no lost paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children they can take music seriously and also learn a trade that pays the rent. Thinking AGI in 2036 and guitar-playing robots around 2039 give us time, but they are not a reason to gamble the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when thinking AGI arrives and about 56 when capable robots follow. A decade helps with training, but our savings are still thin today and I will not be near an easy retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the firm's dates and two pupils this year, and put extra lesson money against the electricity arrears. Over the decade I'd take the maintenance certificate only if a local employer confirms it is needed and a grant covers tuition without lost paid hours; in the first year after 2036 I'd apply for open caretaker work if demo fees have fallen and keep the music dates that still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the bills we already have, though the longer clock makes a new job possible. I would sleep better with three mortgage payments saved, not with a headline about 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the decade without spare money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use each paid month to clear the electricity balance and then build a mortgage reserve, if there is anything left. I cannot promise a fixed saving amount while the firm's calls change each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which picture still worries you after ten years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 still scares me most because our children are young and there is no time to qualify for another job. Ten years would help only if training leads to a real vacancy and the fees are covered.

S4.quote: I would sleep better with three mortgage payments saved, not with a headline about 2036.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The demo fee could go while we still owe the same mortgage, and I have too little saved to train for a new job quickly. Written notice from the firm, a temporary payment plan and a grant for a certificate that leads to a real vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what children hear when a parent says work is changing. My children hear us count the mortgage days at the kitchen table, even when we try to talk quietly.

headlineQuote: My children hear us count the mortgage days at the kitchen table, even when we try to talk quietly.
portrait: Victor is a **43-year-old junior guitarist** with secondary schooling, still learning while playing, recording demos and teaching two beginners.
His **partner and two children** rely on variable shop and music pay to meet a mortgage with less than a month saved.
He **never uses AI** and has few similar jobs nearby; lost demos would hit grocery money quickly.
Even with ten years, he needs **grant-funded training**, a real caretaker vacancy and a mortgage reserve.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could remove demo pay before he can qualify for replacement work.
whatWouldHelp: Written **job notice** and a temporary mortgage payment plan would buy time after cancelled dates.
A **training grant** tied to a real caretaker vacancy would let him study without losing paid hours.
